===== FILE 15996__1.docx =====
Comments to  Docket (VA-2025-VHA-0073)  Department of Veterans Affairs Reproductive Health Services.
I wish to share my concern for the proposed reinstatement of the full exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling from the benefits package for our Veterans and their families.    If the purpose of this proposal is to ensure that the VA provides only medical services needed to our nation's heroes and their families, then I feel that this proposal misses the mark.
A full exclusion on abortion and abortion counseling for a veteran whose life is at risk during her pregnancy fails to support her needs.   While we all hope for healthy welcomed babies to be delivered from our veterans, we know that sometimes things do not go as planned.  Sometimes the mother’s life may be in significant danger and appropriate care is needed to save the veteran’s life.  Sometimes the fetus is not viable and maintaining pregnancy puts the mother at risk of death.   And when a nonviable child is delivered- families go through heart retching time watching their child die an inevitable death.  No one “needs” to be in these situations.  Without this needed reproductive care- women and veterans will be more likely to die unnecessarily.   Data from states with strict abortion laws versus states with supportive reproductive care demonstrates clearly the impact of excluding abortion and abortion consultation to the women of these states.  Please refer to this Tulane report looking at data from 2015 to 2018.  Overall, women were found to be 7% more likely to die in states with restrictive abortion laws prior. 
Since implementing more restrictive abortion bans, women have died being denied care because doctors fear prosecution due to unclear guidance from regulators.  For example in Texas, Josseli Barnica, a 28-year-old mother from Honduras, waited 40 hours in a Texas hospital while doctors monitored her fetal heartbeat during an inevitable miscarriage at 17 weeks. Despite wanting to terminate the pregnancy to prevent infection, Barnica was told it would be a crime. She died of sepsis with “retained products of conception,” two days after finally delivering.
This proposal offers no exceptions for the life of the mother or for rape or incest.  All scenarios which would bring needless horror to the mother and her family.
In conclusion, this proposal is a harmful change failing to meet the needs of our heroic veterans and their families.   All veterans and their families should be able to get the care that they need.
